Your identity is a key you hold — nothing to company that can read your messages or see who you talk to.

Most messengers ask for a phone number, route every message through their servers, and
keep a record of who talks to whom. Wisp does none of that. There is no account, no
directory, and no server that holds your messages or your contacts.

An identity is an Ed25519 keypair, backed up by a 12-word recovery phrase. Peers find
each other over a shared Kademlia DHT, verify each other with a safety number, and
exchange end-to-end encrypted messages — directly when both are online, through a blind
relay when NAT blocks a direct path, or via rotating encrypted dead-drops when the
recipient is offline. Relays and DHT nodes are assumed adversarial: they see only opaque
blobs at unguessable addresses and learn nothing.

Wisp always takes the cheapest path that works, and the relay drops out whenever it isn't needed:

Latest builds are on the Releases page.
Direct download links (always point to the newest release):

Linux: tar -xzf wisp-linux-x64.tar.gz && cd bundle && ./wisp
Windows: extract the zip anywhere and run wisp.exe (keep the folder together).

On Android you may need to allow "install from unknown sources." On first launch, Wisp
generates your identity and shows a 12-word recovery phrase — write it down. It is
the only way to restore your identity, and no one can recover it for you.

Prerequisites: the Flutter SDK, the
Rust toolchain, and — on Linux — the GTK 3, libsecret, and
libnotify development packages.

The Rust protocol core lives in core/; run its tests with cargo test from that
directory.

Wisp uses only well-established cryptography: Ed25519, X25519, Noise XX
(Noise_XX_25519_ChaChaPoly_SHA256), ChaCha20-Poly1305, and the Signal Double Ratchet
with header encryption.

Protected: message content (end-to-end, forward-secret); the social graph (rotating,
derived drop addresses); central seizure (no server holds messages or contacts); takedown
(clients route around blocked relays and bootstrap nodes).

Not fully solved: a global passive adversary may correlate the timing of a write and a
matching read; endpoint compromise defeats any wire encryption; bootstrap dependence is
the softest censorship point.

The claim is not "no servers." It is "no trusted party, and no single point that can read
you, link you, or be leaned on to make you stop."

Wisp is in beta. The core protocol is built and proven on the real internet — identity
and crypto, discovery by WispID, NAT traversal, live relayed sessions, the dead-drop
mailbox, offline delivery across a device restart, and identity binding with safety
numbers. Expect rough edges while it's tested on real devices and networks.

title: Exclusive-Thousands of children, sponsors arrested by ICE after tips from US child migrant agency
description: Aurora's 6-year-old daughter arrived at the U.S. border alone and spent more than half a year in a child migrant shelter while her mother, who was already in the
fullText:
July 28 (Reuters) - Aurora's 6-year-old daughter arrived at the U.S. border alone and spent more than half a year in a child migrant shelter while her mother, who was already in the country, worked to get her out.

The two were finally reunited in late March.

"We were overjoyed," said Aurora, 24, who like others in this story spoke on the condition they be identified only by their first names.

Days later, however, mother and daughter were detained by Immigration and ‌Customs Enforcement and sent to a family detention center in Texas, records show.

They are among more than 12,000 people arrested by U.S. immigration authorities following tips from the Office of Refugee Resettlement during President Donald Trump's second term, according to internal government data ‌reviewed exclusively by Reuters.

ORR was created in 1980 to resettle refugees fleeing war and persecution. Since the early 2000s, the agency has also been charged with housing unaccompanied migrant children arriving at the U.S.-Mexico border, like Aurora's daughter.

The care of these children has historically been walled off from immigration enforcement. A 2008 law sought to ensure they were placed ​in the least restrictive setting and released from detention as soon as safely possible, regardless of their sponsors' legal status.

That meant migrant families could be reunited without fear of being targeted by ICE, even if they were in the country illegally.

The Trump administration has taken a drastically different approach. Since January 2025, the data shows, ORR has shared more than 460,000 "leads" with ICE about unaccompanied children, their sponsors -- usually parents or other relatives -- and additional household members, leaving them vulnerable to detention and deportation.

While Reuters and others have reported on the growing cooperation between ORR and ICE, this story is the first to reveal the scale of the information shared for immigration enforcement.

Interviews with migrant families, legal advocates and current and former U.S. officials illustrate the far-reaching implications of this policy shift and its human toll.

Jen Smyers, who served as deputy director of ORR during the Biden administration, said safeguards against data sharing with ICE have ‌been "completely reversed."

"They are weaponizing a child welfare program for the purposes of more deportations," she said.

In ⁠a statement to Reuters, ORR said it "plays no role in the apprehension of children," referring questions about immigration enforcement to the Department of Homeland Security, ICE's parent agency.

In response to questions from Reuters, DHS said that during Trump's second term "ORR has provided ICE Homeland Security Investigations with potential investigative leads," as part of an effort to locate unaccompanied children who were placed with "unvetted sponsors," including some with criminal records.

Aurora entered the United ⁠States illegally two years ago in search of work and safety.

She left her daughter with family in their rural Mexican village, fearing she was too young for the dangerous desert crossing.

Aurora found a job as a house cleaner in Mississippi. Last August, she said, a relative brought her daughter to the border and left her to surrender to immigration agents, a common strategy among families seeking reunification.

Officials transferred the girl to a migrant children's shelter and Aurora began the vetting process to get her out.

Over the course of six months, she provided the agency with reams of documentation, including a DNA test. She had no criminal record, documents show.

Under ​Trump, ​the screening process for sponsors now includes a number of extra steps, including requiring fingerprints of all household members. As a consequence, the amount of time unaccompanied ​children spend in custody has increased from an average of 30 days in fiscal year 2024 to 194 ‌days in June 2026, according to ORR figures.

ORR declined to comment on specific cases but said its increased vetting is meant to shield children from harm.

The day before being reunited with her daughter, Aurora said, immigration agents visited her at home, asked about the girl, and told her to report to an ICE office the following week.

At that appointment, Aurora recounted, agents "asked me if I had any problems in the U.S. and I said 'no, because I haven't done anything wrong. All I do is work.'"

She and her daughter were detained at the appointment, records show, and sent to a family detention center in Dilley, Texas.

They were there for three weeks. Upon their release, Aurora was fitted with an ankle monitor and instructed to report for regular check-ins pending the outcome of her immigration court case, records show. DHS confirmed details of Aurora's detention and release, saying she had admitted to being "illegally smuggled across the border."

While she was inside, her landlord in Mississippi evicted her and threw out her belongings. So mother and daughter headed to California, where a friend offered to put them up.

Aurora says she fears they will soon be deported.

At night sometimes, her daughter "gets up ‌and cries, thinking she is still detained," her mother said.

Aurora and her daughter are at least together. Other families have been separated again.

Marleny and her ​youngest son fled violence in Guatemala in 2023. They crossed the U.S. border illegally and settled in Texas, where she cleaned construction sites.

Her older son, Victor, stayed with family ​back home. When his uncle was killed, he too decided to make the journey north and turned himself in to U.S. border ​agents.

After four months in ORR custody, Victor was released in late April, the night before his 18th birthday, records show. The family had a party to celebrate.

"I was so happy," Marleny said. "I didn't know then what God had ‌in store for me."

To get Victor out, she provided ORR with extensive documentation for both her and her ​partner, she said, including tax records and fingerprints. Because they had no ​criminal record -- they were "clean clean clean," she said -- she had no qualms about sharing the information.

Two months after Victor was released, though, ICE agents arrested Marleny and her partner at gunpoint as they were getting in their car to go to work.

In response to questions, DHS told Reuters that ICE was executing a criminal search warrant on Marleny's "roommate" - an apparent reference to her partner. DHS did not answer follow-up questions about the nature of the alleged crime or how they had located him.

Seeing the guns was traumatic, Marleny said, ​reminding her of the violence she left behind in Guatemala.

A neighbor who witnessed the arrest alerted Victor, ‌who was in the family's apartment with his 6-year-old brother. In tears, he called a legal assistant at the Galveston-Houston Immigrant Representation Project.

"We've seen so many sponsors arrested and collateral arrests with them," said Alexa Sendukas, a managing attorney with GHIRP.

Victor ​is now caring for his little brother alone. He was due in court after his mother was arrested, but said he forgot to show up in the chaos that followed.

Now facing a deportation order, he hopes to find a lawyer to ​reopen his immigration case.

"I need to keep moving forward," he said.

title: Trump administration plans to end Medicare drug plan subsidy, WSJ reports
description: July 28 () - The Trump administration plans to end a subsidy program that helped hold premiums for Medicare ‌drug plans, the Wall Street Journal reported on Tuesday, ‌citing government officials. The ...
fullText:
July 28 (Reuters) - The Trump administration plans to end a subsidy program that helped hold premiums for Medicare ‌drug plans, the Wall Street Journal reported on Tuesday, ‌citing government officials.

The program, expected to provide insurers with roughly $3.6 billion in subsidies ​this year to cushion Medicare Part D premium increases, will not be renewed beyond 2026, the report said.

Medicare Part D, which provides prescription drug coverage to millions of Medicare beneficiaries through private insurance ‌plans, is a key ⁠component of the federal health program for seniors.

Rising healthcare costs remain a growing concern in the ⁠U.S., particularly for older Americans living on fixed incomes. Nearly 25 million people were enrolled in standalone Medicare Part D prescription drug ​plans in ​2026, according to data from ​health policy research group ‌KFF.

The Journal quoted an administration official who said the additional subsidies gave insurers an incentive to raise premiums because the government would absorb much of the added cost. The official also said the subsidies were no longer necessary, saying that other measures ‌aimed at keeping Medicare Part D ​costs in check remain in place.

The Department ​of Health and Human ​Services, which oversees the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid ‌Services (CMS), did not immediately respond ​to a Reuters ​request for comment.

The administration official told the Journal that about a quarter of Medicare Part D beneficiaries would see ​their premiums remain ‌unchanged or decline next year, while roughly 30% would face ​monthly increases of less than $10.

title: Collins says State Department will reinstate funding for global humanitarian vaccine alliance
description: Sen. Susan Collins (R-Maine) said Tuesday that the State Department is set to reinstate funding for a global humanitarian vaccine program after the Trump administration previously paused the program. ...
fullText:
Sen. Susan Collins (R-Maine) said Tuesday that the State Department is set to reinstate funding for a global humanitarian vaccine program after the Trump administration previously paused the program.

"It is welcome news that following our recent outreach, the State Department has committed to contributing the full $600 million for GAVI, the Vaccine Alliance," Collins said in a Tuesday press release.

"I have worked to ensure that the Department uses this funding Congress appropriated to replenish U.S. funding to GAVI, an organization that plays a critical role in averting the spread of preventable diseases globally and stopping outbreaks before they reach U.S. borders," she added.

Secretary of State Marco Rubio indicated last month that the United States might restart funding for GAVI, a global humanitarian vaccine alliance, going back on a decision from Health and Human Services (HHS) Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. to halt the money due to vaccine concerns.

The State Department head told members of the Senate Foreign Relations Committee that his department had been taking back control of American relations with GAVI, an organization that provides developing countries with vaccines.

According to Rubio, President Trump asked Kennedy to "play a leading role" when it came to the GAVI funding decision "because of the strongly held views with regards to vaccine safety, and he wanted them to conduct some reforms."

A significant part of Gavi's budget has historically come from Congress, with the State Department traditionally overseeing funding for the organization. However, Kennedy and the Department of Health and Human Services held up $600 million in funding that had previously been appropriated due to vaccines he thought were not safe.

title: Exclusive-Iran to get Chinese shoulder-launched missile systems in weeks, sources say
description: Iran is expected to receive within weeks a first shipment out of up to 400 Chinese-made shoulder-fired air-defence missile launchers, three sources
fullText:
July 29 (Reuters) - Iran is expected to receive within weeks a first shipment out of up to 400 Chinese-made shoulder-fired air-defence missile launchers, three sources familiar with the deal told Reuters, as it rebuilds its defences amid war with the United States.

The purchase, valued at $60-70 million, ‌is one of Tehran's largest-known efforts to strengthen its short-range air defences since the outbreak of its war with the U.S. and Israel, which exposed gaps in ‌Iran's ability to protect military sites and strategic infrastructure.

The contract covers the purchase of between 300 and 400 man-portable air defence systems (MANPADS), including Chinese-made QW-12 and FN-16 missiles, the sources said.

The deal was signed with Zhongqing Baoshang International ​Investment, a Hong Kong-based company that the sources said was acting as an intermediary between the Iranian side and the Chinese supplier.

IRAN NEEDS TO REARM AFTER MONTHS OF WAR

The sources spoke on condition of anonymity because of the sensitivity of the matter. Iran's foreign ministry did not immediately reply to a request for comment.

China's Foreign Ministry said: "The relevant reports are completely groundless. China has consistently played a role in promoting peace and ending the conflict."

Beijing-based Zhong Qing Bao Shang Group, the parent company of Zhongqing Baoshang International Investment, did not immediately respond to an email request for comment ‌on Tuesday.

Iran needs to rearm after months of fighting in which ⁠the U.S. and Israel have struck facilities linked to its missile, drone and air-defence programmes, and Tehran responded with barrages of ballistic missiles and drones.

The conflict has highlighted the challenge of defending fixed military and strategic sites against advanced aircraft and precision-guided weapons.

Washington abruptly suspended two weeks of ⁠bombardment on Saturday, but President Donald Trump said strikes would resume if negotiations failed to end the five-month-old conflict, which has in theory been in a state of ceasefire since April.

The delivery of hundreds of MANPADS would significantly expand Iran's inventory of short-range air-defence weapons and underscore how military ties with China are deepening.

The sources cautioned that, although the agreement had been signed, delivery schedules, quantities and other ​implementation ​details could still change.

Under a plan agreed by the parties, deliveries will initially be by air from ​Urumqi in western China, then transiting through Pakistan to Iran, according to ‌the sources, who did not clarify whether the transfers would take place by air or by road.

Pakistan's military public relations wing ISPR said: "Speculations of Pakistan being involved in supply of Air Defence weapons to Iran from China are absolutely concocted and false." A spokesperson for the Pakistani Foreign Ministry did not respond to requests for comment.

CHINA AND IRAN EXPLORE LAND ROUTES FOR DELIVERY, SOURCES SAY

While Iran has invested heavily in the past two decades in missiles, drones and radar, military experts say portable air-defence systems are important because they can be dispersed quickly, operated by small teams and relocated frequently, making them less vulnerable than fixed air-defence batteries.

A European security source said authorities in his country were aware of several contracts under discussion involving ‌the possible sale of QW-series MANPADS to Iran, including QW-12, QW-18 and QW-19 systems.

A second security source, ​in the Middle East, said Iran had been seeking to purchase QW-12 and QW-18 missiles, but they were ​unaware that a deal had already been concluded.

The QW-12 and FN-16 are shoulder-fired, infrared-guided ​surface-to-air missile systems designed to engage low-flying aircraft, helicopters and drones. Their mobility allows them to be deployed rapidly around military installations, energy infrastructure ‌and other sensitive sites.

Defence analysts regard the QW-12 as less capable than ​newer QW variants, including the QW-18 and QW-19, ​but say the systems can still provide an effective layer of short-range protection against drones and low-flying targets.

Two Western intelligence sources and an Iranian official said Tehran had also explored the use of overland routes to move Chinese military supplies and dual-use components more discreetly and reduce the risk of disruption.

The procurement highlights the Islamic Republic's ​continuing reliance on a combination of domestic weapons production and foreign ‌suppliers despite years of sanctions and restrictions on defence-related imports.

(Additional reporting by Liz Lee in Beijing, Clare Jim ​in Hong Kong and Rick Noack in IslamabadWriting by Parisa Hafezi; Editing by Kevin Liffey)

title: Republican Ohio governor says Trump’s plans to deport Haitians a ‘mistake’
description: Ohio Gov. Mike DeWine (R) said Monday the Trump administration would be making a “mistake” if it were to deport thousands of Haitian migrants who it has stripped of their temporary protected status (T...
fullText:
Ohio Gov. Mike DeWine (R) said Monday the Trump administration would be making a "mistake" if it were to deport thousands of Haitian migrants who it has stripped of their temporary protected status (TPS).

"It's a mistake. It's not good for the United States and it's not good for the state of Ohio," DeWine told CBS News's Camilo Montoya-Galvez.

Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) plans to ramp up operations to arrest and deport Haitian migrants without legal status, CBS News reported Monday. DeWine, whose state has a significant Haitian diaspora, told the outlet he has "received no notification" of such a plan from ICE.

The Hill has reached out to ICE for comment.

Former Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem ended TPS for Haitians last year, and the Supreme Court upheld that move last month. Prior to the expiration of TPS on Monday, there were roughly 330,000 Haitians in the U.S. with that status, with 14,000 living in Ohio, according to a January report from the immigration advocacy group Fwd.us.

DeWine has long defended Haitian migrants, saying they contribute to his state's economy. He made the same argument to CBS News, saying Haitians "have helped" cities such as Springfield.

During the 2024 campaign, President Trump and Vice President Vance joined those falsely accusing Haitians in Springfield of eating people's pets.

"Springfield has been making a real comeback," DeWine said. "The Haitians who are living there and [are] employed there, they came there to work and they came there because there were jobs that were not being filled by other people."

The governor later added, "These are people who have opened restaurants. They've opened other businesses. They're rehabbed houses. They've created jobs, as well as filled jobs.

"So to lose them and have them not be able to work anymore and possibly taken out of this country, it's frankly a blow to Springfield and a blow to the state of Ohio."

Haitian TPS holders contributed an estimated $5.9 billion to the U.S. economy each year, including $91 million to Springfield, according to the report from Fwd.us. They also pay more than $1.5 billion per year in federal, payroll, state and local taxes combined.

If the Trump administration deports Haitians back to Haiti, they would be sending those migrants to a country the State Department advises Americans against traveling to due to the risk of crime, terrorism, kidnapping, unrest and limited healthcare.

The Obama administration first extended TPS to Haitians in the wake of the devastating 2010 earthquake in the Caribbean island.

DeWine said the administration would be sending Haitians "back to hell" by deporting them to their home country.

"Very few of these Haitians will voluntarily go back to Haiti," the GOP governor added. "If they have to leave, they'll go someplace else. They want to work. They want to support their family. They don't want to go back to Haiti."

title: Three stabbed in flat before jumping out of window
description: A man and two women, who were all injured, are arrested on suspicion of causing grievous bodily harm.
fullText:
Three people were stabbed during a fight in a flat in Nottingham before sustaining further injuries when they jumped out of a window.

Nottinghamshire Police said the altercation happened at a property in Wasnidge Walk in St Ann's at about 22:15 BST on Monday.

A man, 27, was found outside the flat while two women, 26 and 31, were found injured in Union Road in the city centre. They are all now in hospital receiving treatment for potentially life-altering injuries, police added.

All three have since been arrested on suspicion of causing grievous bodily harm.

Ch Insp Kylie Davies said: "All three are currently receiving treatment in hospital, having appeared to have sustained stab wounds and other injuries at various stages of this incident, which was isolated and poses no threat to the wider public.

"As I say, we're still trying to piece together exactly what happened here, so in the meantime, we'd ask people to please share any information they have, however small or insignificant it may seem.

"In addition to anyone who witnessed this take place, we also want to hear from anyone who has CCTV, doorbell, dashcam, or mobile phone footage that could assist our ongoing inquiries."

Listen to BBC Radio Nottingham on Sounds and follow BBC Nottingham on Facebook, on X, or on Instagram. Send your story ideas to eastmidsnews@bbc.co.uk or via WhatsApp on 0808 100 2210.

title: Putin, Russia put on notice as Senate takes crucial step to grind down the Kremlin’s war machine
description: The bipartisan sanctions bill targets Russian oil and gas while adding Iran penalties, with up to 500% tariffs and 100% on buyers like China.
fullText:
The Senate took its first major step in fulfilling one of the late Sen. Lindsey Graham's biggest desires: levying bone-crushing sanctions against Russia.

A bipartisan swell carried the sanctions package through its first hurdle on an 86-12 vote, which has gone through several iterations in the time since it was first formulated by Graham and Sen. Richard Blumenthal, D-Conn. He explained that at its core, the package was designed to stop purchases of Russian oil and gas that was "fueling Putin's war machine."

"Ukraine's fight is our fight," Blumenthal said. "Nobody believed that more deeply and passionately than Lindsey Graham. He lived it, and this vote is a step forward."

Lindsey Graham's Final Mission Nears Finish Line As World Leaders Gather To Honor Him

The colossal vote also marks a huge victory on the floor for Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., who over the summer has managed to pass or advance two major bills with a massive wave of bipartisan support on the Senate floor, even during starkly partisan times in upper chamber.

And the package that survived Tuesday night, just hours after lawmakers, world leaders and family said their last Washington, D.C., goodbyes to the longtime senator has once again been revamped.

A bipartisan group led by Blumenthal and Sen. Darline Graham, R-S.C., who picked up her older brother's sanctions crusade, announced that a deal had been reached to rename the package in honor of the late lawmaker, and tack on additional sanctions against Iran.

Lawmakers argue that the best way to remember Graham, and cement his legacy into law, is to pass the newly-minted Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act, particularly as a symbol of his ferocious support for Ukraine.

Lindsey Graham's Sister Carries On Late Senator's Work, Becoming South Carolina's First Female Senator

Sen. Jon Husted, R-Ohio, told Fox News Digital that "literally the first conversation I ever had with Lindsey Graham was about Russia sanctions."

"I know he was very passionate about this and I know that sanctions are one of the best tools we have for bringing wars to an end without having to commit any of our military," Husted said.

The bill, as Blumenthal noted, still focuses on kneecapping Russian President Vladimir Putin's war effort by targeting Moscow's top financial gainer: oil and gas sales.

Bringing The War To Putin's Front Door: Is Ukraine's Energy Strike Strategy Working?

But it also extends sanction authority against Iran that hampers funding to the country's weapons and energy sectors as the administration and negotiators abroad seek to find a long-lasting peace agreement for the war in the Middle East.

Also, still in the legislation are targeted sanctions against Putin, Russian officials and Russian military leaders, up to 500% tariffs on Russian imports, tariffs of up to 100% on countries buying Russian energy, like China and India.

It also gives President Donald Trump flexibility for when to turn off some aspects of the sanctions, among others.

Sen. Katie Britt, R-Ala., one of the original backers of the sanctions package, is already putting pressure on the House to make a move on the legislation. The lower chamber left until the end of August last week.

"I am hopeful that when we get this across the finish line, which is going to happen in a big way, that the House will come back immediately and pass this legislation," Britt said.

Meanwhile, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, a close ally of Graham's, made the journey to Washington to attend his funeral, and meet with President Donald Trump and lawmakers in the process to push the sanctions bill and a deal for more anti-ballistic defenses in the war against Russia.

Zelenskyy said on X that, "First and foremost, I offered President Trump our condolences on the passing of Lindsey Graham. He was a true friend of Ukraine."

"The President and I discussed licenses for Patriot interceptor production and several other ideas that could help," Zelenskyy said. "We also spoke about diplomacy – it's important that the diplomatic process be reinvigorated."

And Zelenskyy, after his closed-door meeting with lawmakers, went to the viewing gallery in the Senate to watch vote, which after many stops and starts, finally showed signs of progress.

Original article

title: Police probe 'unexplained' deaths of man, 43, and woman, 36
description: They were found by emergency services in the Houston area on Monday morning.
fullText:
Police are investigating the deaths of a man and a woman after their bodies were found in Renfrewshire.

The man, who was 43, and the 36-year-old woman were discovered in the Houston area on Monday morning.

Officers said their deaths were being treated as "unexplained" and post-mortem examinations would be carried out.

They said their inquiries were continuing but there was nothing to suggest anyone else had been involved.

Police said they received a report of concerns for a person in Corsliehill Road at about 07:50 on Monday.

When the emergency services arrived at the scene, they found the bodies of the man and woman nearby.

A spokesperson said: "The deaths are being treated as unexplained and post-mortem examinations will be carried out in due course.

"Extensive inquiries are continuing to establish the full circumstances. At this time, there is nothing to suggest anyone else has been involved.

"Their relatives are aware and are being supported by specialist officers."

The Scottish Ambulance Service said they were called to nearby Barochan Road at 08:33.

A spokesperson added: "Four special operations response teams, two ambulances and one critical care team were dispatched to the scene."

title: Longevity guru Bryan Johnson offers 3 tips for optimum sleep
description: The longevity guru said he considers his resting heart rate before bed his most important biomarker.
fullText:
(NewsNation) — Wealthy biohacker Bryan Johnson, who's spending a fortune in hopes of significantly prolonging his lifespan, offers three simple tips that he uses to optimize his sleep.

The so-called longevity guru said he considers his resting heart rate before bed the most important biomarker that can help him achieve his long-term goal of living well past 100 years.

"I'll look at my heart rate and see how many times it's beating per minute. It is the best indicator of how I'm going to sleep and of my overall health," Johnson told Chris Cuomo during a televised town hall Tuesday about AI that included the topic of wellness.

The 48-year-old Johnson offered three examples of things he does to control the key metric: He stops eating four hours before bedtime; turns off his electronic screens 30 minutes to 60 minutes before turning in; and refrains from caffeine after noon.

"These really basic practices dramatically lower my heart rate, they improve my sleep, which then improves my willpower, allows me to eat better and exercise," Johnson said. "So, really simple, basic things have a dramatic ability to improve your health and wellness."

A resting heart rate of 60 to 100 beats per minute is considered normal, although athletes can have resting heart rates that are closer to 40 beats per minute, according to the Mayo Clinic.

Johnson, who made his fortune through digital payment companies, has become known for trying to reduce his biological age through strict diet, physical training and medical tracking. Media accounts characterize him as trying to live forever, but Johnson, in remarks Tuesday, emphasized the idea of pushing boundaries.

"Five years ago," he said, "I started on this quest with the basic question: Are we the first generation who won't die? Now, that does not mean immortality. It means, will we begin extending our lifespans to 80, 85, 90, 100, 120, 130? Then at some point we say, 'Huh, is it going to just keep on going?' What do we do?"

title: 15-year-old arrested at Seattle food festival shooting was armed with a ghost gun, police say
description: The 15-year-old arrested after a shootout at a food festival near Seattle’s Space Needle over the weekend was armed with a ghost gun with an extended magazine, police said Tuesday.  Police Chief Shon ...
fullText:
SEATTLE (AP) — The 15-year-old arrested after a shootout at a food festival near Seattle's Space Needle over the weekend was armed with a ghost gun with an extended magazine, police said Tuesday.

Police Chief Shon Barnes told a news conference that the weapon was a 9 mm gun from Polymer80 — a now-defunct company that was once a leading manufacturer of ghost gun parts.

Investigators also recovered two other weapons and 14 shell casings that had been fired by weapons of two different calibers, he said.

The shooting in the waning hours of the three-day Bite of Seattle festival left three people dead, including a 19-year-old gunman, and at least four people injured, including a toddler. Authorities say they believe the violence was gang-related, and they are reviewing any available surveillance video and interviewing victims and witnesses in an effort to identify others who may have been involved.

An eighth person with a possible gunshot wound checked themself into a Seattle hospital after the shooting, but checked out before investigators could conduct an interview, Barnes said. Legal obstacles have prevented detectives from obtaining the patient's identity, he added. It's unclear if the injury was related to the festival shooting or whether the person might have been involved in it, but Barnes asked for the person to come forward and speak with investigators.

Ghost guns are privately made — often homemade — firearms that lack serial numbers used to trace them. They have often been purchased without a background check. Law enforcement officials say ghost guns, including those made with 3D printers, have been used in violent crimes across the U.S.

Lawsuits and state-level bans eventually pushed Polymer80 out of business in 2024, and last year, the U.S. Supreme Court upheld a rule adopted under former President Joe Biden requiring companies to treat gun kits like other firearms by adding serial numbers, running background checks, and verifying that buyers are 21 or older.

The weapon the 15-year-old had been shooting when he surrendered to police was equipped with an extended 33-round magazine, Barnes said. The magazine still had 19 rounds in it.

At the scene Sunday night, police also recovered a 9 mm handgun that they do not believe was used in the shooting.

And on Monday, as food vendors were allowed to return to the area to clean up and collect their equipment, a third weapon was discovered: a Glock 45 model 9 mm with a switch allowing it to fire fully automatically, Barnes said. Police believe that gun was fired during the shooting. It had an extended 40-round magazine, with 21 rounds remaining in it.

In a document filed in juvenile court in Seattle on Monday, police said they believed there were at least three shooters: the 15-year-old, an acquaintance who died at the scene and "at least one other unknown suspect." Authorities had earlier said they believed there were two.

A judge on Monday ordered the 15-year-old to be held in juvenile detention for investigation of assault and firearms charges pending further hearings. The King County prosecutor's office said it expected to receive the case from police on Wednesday for a charging decision. Hong Tran, a public defender assigned to the teen's case, declined to comment in an email to The Associated Press on Tuesday.

The King County Medical Examiner's Office on Monday identified the dead as Carlos Israel Sanchez Villalba, 44; Ashley Whitehead, 56; and Junior Cee Niko Semo, 19.

Villalba was a husband and father of three known for his kindness and willingness to help others, according to a GoFundMe campaign launched Monday to help his family with funeral expenses. He died from a gunshot wound to his torso, while Whitehead died from a gunshot to her pelvis and Semo died from multiple gunshot wounds, according to the medical examiner's office.

Whitehead had just moved to Washington from Alabama a year ago and was enjoying the festival with one of her adult daughters when she was shot, her cousin Michelle Whitehead told The Associated Press. She was taken to the hospital and died in surgery, she said.

Ashley Whitehead adored her two adult daughters, and also loved nature and arts and crafts, her cousin said.

"I would consider her just a free spirit. She had the best sense of humor, the best gorgeous smile," she said.

During a vigil Monday night at the center, Michelle Whitehead stood among dozens of others with a sign that said "Whitehead Strong" as the group held a moment of silence and raised up flashlights on their phones to honor those that had been killed. Candles and flowers were arranged around them.

title: The 23-year-old teacher leading lesson on stripping bowls' stigma
description: Scotland's Sophie McGrouther is targeting a Commonwealth Games medal in bowls while also aiming to break the stigma attached to the sport she loves.
fullText:
A 23-year-old walking out to Mountains by Biffy Clyro is not the picture many people will paint when they think of bowls.

But that will be the scene in hall three at the SEC Centre on Wednesday when Scotland's Sophie McGrouther begins her women's singles campaign.

Despite being the youngest member of Scotland's bowls team, primary school teacher McGrouther has set her sights high.

Given she was the world indoor champion aged 21, why shouldn't she aim for a slab of metal come the weekend?

There'd certainly be worse things than a Commonwealth Games medal to show her class as part of a 'what did you do during your summer holidays?' lesson.

But there's a bigger picture here too.

Introducing new eyes, inspiring the next generation and breaking the stigma attached to the sport she loves is at the forefront of McGrouther's mind over the next few days in Glasgow.

Bee Gees at bowls as Scotland Para-mixed pairs retain gold

'Mariah Cleggy' channels Messi to swim to gold for Scotland

All the latest from Scotland at the Games

When anyone of a certain age says they play bowls, they face a barrage of questions. At the crux of most of them is, 'why?'

Then throw in the comments about it being a boring, old man's game. The record has never changed. Until the DJ at the SEC has their way...

McGrouther has been asked time and time again. Her answers, though, may be a little surprising.

Usually parents or grandparents can be pointed to, but the Fife native didn't have anyone hauling her along to her local club. She, quite literally, went along herself.

After being introduced to the game aged 10 via a taster session at school, she made the decision to have a go at Abbeyview Bowling Club. And to the surprise of many at the time, she stuck at it. Thank goodness she did.

"I used to go to the club after school and they would laugh at me coming in on my scooter and they'd be like, 'who is she?'," McGrouther told BBC Sport Scotland.

"For me, it's the social aspect, the friends that you meet all over the world that really that keeps it going.

"I definitely missed out on a lot of events and things because I was always focused on training, but it's just nice that it's all been worth it."

Having travelled the world with her bowls in tow, she's acutely aware of the opportunities the game has given her. She's even more switched on to the impact a Games can have.

Even though she had just started throwing bowls - and already finding them very close to the jack - she was giddy in the grandstands at Kelvingrove 12 years ago, cheering on Paul Foster and Alex 'Tattie' Marshall as they won gold in the men's pairs at the 2014 Commonwealth Games.

It's "unbelievable" for her to now be competing alongside her heroes at these home Games, which are not only different in being played indoors.

There are two big glitter balls on arrival at the bowls hall, while the Bee Gees were playing during McGrouther's team-mates' Para-mixed pairs B2-B3 win on Tuesday.

This is a revamped bowls, searching for the next superstar in the stand.

"If I can inspire one other little girl to go and take up bowls, that whole chain reaction that they end up in a similar situation to me 12 years later, that would be such a big achievement for me," she added.

"Just trying to move away from the stigma bowls has, because the days of traditional clothing and only the older generation playing are gone.

"We are moving away from that and trying to keep the sport alive and growing for the younger audience."

There is no doubt there will be a young, budding audience in West Lothian where McGrouther teaches, though.

All at Winchburgh Primary School were getting in the Games spirit before the summer holidays, to the degree the bowler felt "like a celebrity" in the corridors.

"There was a proper buzz around the whole school, we did an all-in Glasgow 2026 campaign throughout with lots of competitions and I definitely felt like a celebrity walking through the corridors," she added.

"They were saying like, 'Miss McGrouther, you're famous, you're going to the Commonwealth Games!'

"Hopefully it's been inspiring for them, I know a lot of them perhaps hadn't heard of the Commonwealth Games or it wasn't as relevant to them, but bringing that into the classroom for them, they were able to see it.

"Some of my kids are coming to watch next week and just introducing the younger generation to not only bowls, but the other nine sports, is so important."

The finishing touches are being applied to the supportive posters by her school kids - that she knows will "leave her emotional" - but this is only the beginning of not just her Games journey, but a new look for her sport.

title: Birmingham & Preston - Barcelona's unlikely UK camp
description: Barcelona will be training at St George's Park this week and taking on Championship sides Birmingham City and Preston.
fullText:
As Premier League clubs jet off to the Far East and the United States, Barcelona have made the Midlands their home.

Manager Hansi Flick has brought his La Liga champions to St George's Park in Staffordshire for a training camp this week as their pre-season preparations continue.

Barca's eight World Cup winners - including Lamine Yamal - remain on a break after their triumph with Spain this month, but new signing Karim Adeyemi is included after his summer move from Borussia Dortmund.

In addition to Lamine Yamal, his Spain team-mates Ferran Torres, Joan Garcia, Eric Garcia, Pau Cubarsi, Gavi, Dani Olmo, Pedri and Lamine Yamal are also on a post-World Cup break.

Two friendlies against Championship sides await - against Birmingham at St Andrew's on Friday, and against Preston behind closed doors at St George's Park on Monday - with the knock-on effects of the World Cup playing a part in the organising of those matches.

Barcelona ruled out a long-haul tour to the United States because of the World Cup schedule.

As well as missing their Spain stars, they are without another six senior internationals, including England's Anthony Gordon following his £80m move from Newcastle.

Brazil's Raphinha, France's Jules Kounde and Uruguay's Ronald Araujo are absent too.

Having opted out of a transatlantic tour, Barca had spent a large part of the year looking at their options, trying to work around the fact that their players return at different times because of the World Cup.

Birmingham had been speaking to the club for a number of months as they looked to boost their own profile.

The Blues, who missed out on the Championship play-offs last season, have promotion ambitions under chairman Tom Wagner and minority owner and seven-time Super Bowl champion Tom Brady.

Barca decided to come to the UK as they wanted a good standard of opposition as part of their pre-season programme, having previously spent time at St George's Park in 2014 - before they won the Treble of La Liga, Copa del Rey and the Champions League - and then in 2016.

Roma have trained there in the past, while Nantes, Fiorentina and Rangers used the facility last summer.

The 30-man squad flew to Birmingham on Monday before training early evening in the Midlands, with Fermín Lopez continuing his recovery from injury.

The midfielder missed out on Spain's World Cup success after breaking his foot against Real Betis in May.

Flick's squad is a mix of senior players, along with others from Barcelona B and the under-19s, including forward Orian Goren who only turned 17 in March.

Netherlands midfielder Frenkie de Jong has travelled despite a knee injury which was expected to keep him out for months.

The 29-year-old damaged the medial collateral ligament in his right knee at the World Cup.

Another surprise inclusion is Marc-Andre ter Stegen, who has been expected to move to Ajax on loan. No deal has been struck so the German goalkeeper has travelled to England and could face Birmingham in Friday's game.

Barca had a double session on Tuesday and are training on the pitch reserved for the England senior team.

After their trip to St Andrew's, Barca will take on Preston behind closed doors at St George's Park next Monday.

Paul Heckingbottom's side started their pre-season with a 4-1 win against Northern Premier League Premier Division side Bamber Bridge at the start of the month.

Barca also travel to Italy for two 45-minute matches against Nottingham Forest and Udinese in the Friuli Venezia Giulia tournament on 8 August.

Barcelona squad: Ter Stegen, Fort, Balde, Araujo, Cortes, Guille Fernandez, Toni Fernandez, Farinas, Abdelkarim, Tommy, Xavi Espart, Yaakobishvili, Adeyemi, Christensen, Fermin, M Casado, Gerard Martin, Roony, Tunkara, Torrents, Bernal, Gonzalez, Kluivert, Szczesny, Goren, Gistau, Diarra, Pesquer, Rodriguez, De Jong.

title: Englishman, Scotsman, Northern Irishman and Welshman race is no joke
description: Rather than walking into a bar, the quartet who won world relay gold last year now go head to head at the Commonwealth Games.
fullText:
An Englishman, a Northern Irishman, a Scotsman and a Welshman.

Rather than walking into a bar, this quartet won gold for Great Britain in the 4x200m freestyle relay at the 2025 Aquatics World Championships in Singapore.

England's James Guy, Northern Ireland's Jack McMillan, Scotland's Duncan Scott and Wales' Matt Richards came together to deliver for Team GB like swimming's version of rugby's British & Irish Lions.

But almost a year later, the team-mates will race one another for the individual 200m freestyle Commonwealth title.

"It's such a unique relationship. We're all competitors for the individual or team-mates for that 4x200m relay," said Richards.

"Then you throw Commonwealths into the mix and it makes it even more dynamic and different.

"There's a lot of trash talk between us leading up to it which is great fun and always a good laugh."

Is struggling Ramsay-Peaty nearing the end?

Whiston wins gold after ill father makes rare trip

Commonwealth Games medal table and results

So while the friendly rivals are keeping their sense of humour, who will have the last laugh?

Richards has already won three medals at these Games but is still waiting for his first gold.

He and McMillan swim in the same heat on Wednesday as Scotsman Evan Jones and Englishman Tom Dean, who were also part of that world champion relay squad.

"We're all good friends and that camaraderie helps us as team-mates, but also as rivals to push each other," said McMillan.

"We play our roles when it comes the the relay but swimming is an individual sport too."

England's Guy said the chance for Team GB colleagues to go head to head "makes the Commonwealth Games a bit more special".

"It's actually really cool because it's very rare we represent our home nations," he added.

"It's really weird being part of different countries when you're together most of the time as Team GB."

Australia have dominated in the pool so far in these Games but Scott, who has already claimed gold in Glasgow, knows all four team-mates have ambitions to top the podium.

"We go head to head so much at British Championships year in and year out, in season meets, that it's always good fun racing those boys," Scott said.

"Ultimately we all want to see each other swim well," added Richards.

"We just want to see ourselves swim that tiny bit better."

title: Cruz Hewitt - son of Lleyton - wins on senior debut
description: Cruz Hewitt - the 17-year-old son of former world number one Lleyton Hewitt - earned his first ATP victory in his main singles draw debut.
fullText:
Cruz Hewitt - the 17-year-old son of former world number one Lleyton Hewitt - earned his first ATP victory in his main singles draw debut.

The Australian beat fellow qualifier Marcos Giron of the United States 6-3 6-4 in 74 minutes.

His maiden win came at the Washington Open - a competition his father won in 2004.

It was one of his father's 30 career titles, including the 2002 Wimbledon men's singles crown.

"It's a pretty special moment," Hewitt said. "Seeing my dad play this tournament and to get my first tour win, it feels really cool."

Hewitt could next play fellow Australian Alex de Minaur, the top seed and defending Washington champion.

De Minaur faces Greek Stefanos Tsitsipas on Wednesday.

Hewitt junior copied a famous celebration from his father after the victory - a right arm bicep curl.

"He just always did it and when I was little I've just always seen it," Hewitt said. "It's cool to be able to do that now because obviously my dad has been a huge part of where I am today."

The teenager said he was inspired when he saw his father's name on the ring of champions in Washington DC during qualifying.

"It's very surreal," he said. "Kind of inspirational to look up at it as well.

"I do feel pretty comfortable to be at the tournaments. It's pretty exciting because I've dreamed of playing at these tournaments and I've seen behind the scenes and to be in the gym and the locker room with these guys, it's pretty cool."

title: The gold medal-winning Para-swimmer competing in non-disabled race
description: Faye Rogers turned to Para-swimming after an accident. Now she is back where she started and is quicker than ever.
fullText:
For most athletes at these Commonwealth Games, winning a gold medal on the opening night could not be eclipsed.

But when Scotland's Faye Rogers returns to the pool at Tollcross on Wednesday, what happens next is something she will cherish just as much as standing on top of the podium last Friday.

The 23-year-old didn't just win the S10 200 individual medley - she owned it. A winning margin of just over 2.5 seconds is an eternity over four lengths of the pool.

But when she stands on the block for her next event, it will be an entirely different challenge, because Para-athlete Rogers will race the 200m butterfly.

Five years ago, that was her event. And she was good at it. She'd qualified for the Team GB Olympic trials and was set to move to Aberdeen to study as well as train under Patrick Miley, father of Olympian Hannah.

But the day she was due to leave home in Teesside to move to Scotland, Rodgers was involved in a serious car accident on the way to training. She suffered a complex open fracture to her right arm, multiple dislocations, and a severed ulnar nerve.

She was told she would never swim competitively again.

Scotland win three medals in 45 minutes to kick-start Glasgow 2026

'Mariah Cleggy' channels Messi to swim to gold before relay team take bronze

Yet 12 weeks later, Rogers was back in the pool doing rehab. And by summer 2024 she was in Paris winning Paralympic gold. But perhaps the most remarkable thing of all is that she is quicker now than she was pre-accident.

"I never in a million years thought that I could be faster," Rogers, who is unable to straighten her right arm, tells BBC Sport. "Yes, it looks a bit different and there is definitely an impairment there. But I've worked harder, I'm fitter, I'm stronger.

"My message is just 'don't let anyone tell you what you can and can't do'. We're all different. We've all got our own stuff. But I think anything is totally doable if you put your mind to it."

Not many Para-athletes have done what Rogers is about to do.

It was last year that she resolved to put her "big girl pants on" and act upon a notion she'd had for a while to test where she was in the 200m fly. And the first time she did swim it, she realised she was only just a fraction shy of her pre-accident best.

With that, her mind was made up. She spoke to the selectors and it was agreed that, as long as three other athletes did not post fastest times, she could compete at the Commonwealths. They didn't, and Rogers was in.

"I found out a couple of weeks ago and I've been so, so excited ever since," said the Edinburgh University student, for whom making the final would be a huge success.

"There's no pressure. I think it's such a privilege to have the opportunity to stand up there and and to show other people with impairments that, no matter what you are told, and no matter what gets thrown at you, like there's a way through it.

"We quite often get told we can't. And this is my way of proving that we can."

title: Brighton's Welbeck set for Chelsea medical
description: Brighton striker Danny Welbeck is given permission to have a medical at Stamford Bridge as his move to Chelsea moves closer.
fullText:
Chelsea are finalising a move for Brighton striker Danny Welbeck after he was given permission to have a medical at Stamford Bridge.

Welbeck, 35, is set to link up with his new club in Hong Kong next week for pre-season as he prepares to sign a two-year contract.

The move is part of new manager Xabi Alonso's recruitment drive to add experience to Chelsea's squad, which has been the youngest in the Premier League for the past two seasons.

Their focus on youth has been viewed as a factor in their inability to challenge consistently for major honours.

Towards the end of last season's disappointing campaign, when they finished 10th and won nothing, Chelsea co-owner Behdad Eghbali said their recruitment model needed a "tweak".

Since then, Chelsea have made an offer to reunite Sunderland midfielder Granit Xhaka, 34, with Alonso - they won the Bundesliga title together at Bayer Leverkusen in 2024.

They have also signed 26-year-old centre-back Maxence Lacroix from Crystal Palace on a six-year contract, pending an official announcement, while talks continue over a deal for Brentford midfielder Jordan Henderson, 36.

Morgan Rogers, signed for a club record £117m from Aston Villa earlier this month, is also relatively experienced, despite having just turned 24.

The club have also signed 21-year-old full-back Marco Palestra from Atalanta.

Welbeck, formerly of Manchester United and Arsenal, has hit 90 goals in 400 top-flight appearances - and is the leading Premier League scorer at Brighton, who he joined on a free transfer from Watford in 2021.

His arrival would leave Chelsea with six senior strikers on their books as they look to build around Joao Pedro and Welbeck, with others available for loan or sale.

Among those who could leave on either a permanent deal or loan are Nicolas Jackson, Liam Delap and Marc Guiu.

The Blues have also brought in Dutch striker Emmanuel Emegha from sister club Strasbourg this summer and he could remain part of the squad.

title: The athlete who has never held her Olympic medal
description: The story of Cameroon Olympic medallist Madias Ngake's remarkable journey from sleeping rough and seeking asylum to competing for England at Glasgow 2026.
fullText:
Nearly 5,000 miles from her home, somewhere in Cameroon's capital, Madias Ngake suspects that in a drawer which is not hers, lies an Olympic medal which is.

It was awarded to her seven years late, after three weightlifters who finished above her at London 2012 were disqualified for doping offences. She has never held that medal, having never returned to her homeland in the 14 years since first landing in the UK.

Ngake, who is now based in Nottingham, had not planned to stay, but she had not anticipated needing to make a life-changing decision which she perceived to be her only chance of "safety and freedom" from persecution.

During those Games, her sexuality became known. With homosexuality illegal in Cameroon, punishable by imprisonment, genuine "fear" for her life drove the then 20-year-old to disappear from the athletes' village.

"After I finished competing in 2012, staying was not easy, but I had to take a decision for my safety, for my future, because I saw I did not have a future any 

"I'm a lesbian, I love women and it's not allowed in Cameroon. I had to stay here for me to have a good future, good life and not hurt myself if I decide to have a girlfriend."

While she would secure sanctuary, of sorts, by avoiding a return to the African nation, her experiences over the following months were a far cry from the "glamourous" fortnight she had spent at the Olympics.

With no friends, no home and no money, the following months were largely spent on the streets.

Now, 14 years after London 2012, Ngake will make a remarkable return to a major multi-sport event when she competes at the Glasgow 2026 Commonwealth Games for her adopted nation, England.

"This moment means a lot to me," says the weightlifter, who won European bronze for Great Britain earlier this year. "For Team England to have given me this second opportunity, it is amazing."

Ngake was born in Douala, the largest city in Cameroon, around 200 miles to the west of the nation's capital Yaounde.

She is reluctant to reflect too much on that time, having distanced herself from thoughts of her homeland for more than a decade, but it is clear that childhood brought "challenges", many, many challenges. It is also clear that through sport, specifically weightlifting, she found a talent which could elevate her.

Ngake dreamed of not only personal success, but profound change. She aimed to help influence a shift in perceptions around female sport by showcasing the power of strong women in Cameroon.

At the Delhi 2010 Commonwealth Games, the then 18-year-old gave a glimpse of that potential. She placed fourth, achieving the same total as India's bronze medallist Laishram Devi but losing out on a podium place by virtue of weighing more than her rival.

Not that it was of immediate concern. Ngake left that contest on a stretcher, having passed out moments after a successful 121kg lift. It was a disappointing end to her Commonwealth debut, but there was still plenty of pride.

"Not just anybody can qualify for a Commonwealth Games," she smiles. "It means you're strong and, can I say, special?"

With resources limited, a situation not helped by the widely reported corruption scandals within several international federations in Cameroon, attending international competitions was extremely challenging.

As a result, she entered London 2012 with relatively low rank, which meant she was assigned to the B Final, with other athletes not considered to have realistic medal prospects.

However, she not only won the B Final, but lifted considerably more than many in the 'elite' division, securing an overall ranking of sixth. It was an achievement she considered to be "amazing" at the time, long before the results and placements were revised.

There was not time to celebrate that achievement, though. She needed to act quickly.

Exactly how the situation transpired is something, even 14 years on, Ngake is reluctant to discuss, but she is open about the impact of absconding.

"When I decided to stay, sometimes I would sleep on the bus, but when the bus stopped [for the night], I would sleep outside," she recalls with a shrug. "When I wanted to have a shower, I would maybe find a place outside, in public, so to change myself was not too easy."

That period lasted for around two months before she officially applied for asylum and was offered temporary accommodation while her case was reviewed.

Neither the Olympic Games nor any form of sport were in her mind. She was just focused on finding a way to make the UK her home.

Few around the weightlifter knew of her elite performance background and few would have even suspected it as the Olympian settled in to a more low-key existence.

Nearly five years passed before she was able to attain the correct paperwork to take on permanent paid employment. It meant starting at the bottom, but she was happy just to have the opportunity to build.

"At first, I was an office cleaner and yes, that was my full-time job for nine years," the now 34-year-old says. "I was in Leeds, then I moved to Nottingham."

She did not think about the sport she once loved for all that time.

But that changed four years ago.

With Durban stripped of the rights to host the 2022 Commonwealth Games after failing to meet key milestones or provide financial guarantees, Birmingham stepped in.

It meant some of Ngake's former team-mates and coaches from Cameroon would return to the UK themselves and for the first time in a decade she allowed her mind to dwell on weightlifting.

"One of my coaches was still with the team, travelling over for Birmingham 2022 and after he came to stay with me and kept pushing me to start again," she says.

"I'd stopped everything, but he encouraged me and when I did lift a bar again, yes, it felt so natural, it felt right and that was very exciting."

The following year she won gold at the British International and within a further 12 months she not only returned to the international stage, but landed a major career-first, with silver in the snatch discipline at the 2024 World Championships for Great Britain.

As a naturalised athlete, with proven major event medal-winning potential, she was now eligible for UK Sport funding, which soon arrived, enabling Ngake to give up her job as a cleaner and focus on being a full-time athlete.

European honours have followed and she heads into a second Commonwealth Games, 16 years on from her debut in India, as the top seed in the women's 86kg division.

She is joined in the squad line-up by fellow Cameroon-born athlete turned Team England weightlifter Cyrille Tchatchet II. He sought asylum after competing at the Glasgow 2014 Commonwealth Games and will make an emotional return to Scotland later this week.

Their stories are remarkable, but they are acutely aware that not everyone has positive views about asylum seekers. Ngake has strong opinions herself about those from overseas who wish to live in the UK.

"Some people come here, apply for asylum seeker and they are very good people, but some are not good, so there is a mix," she says.

"I'm not going to say I'm good or bad, but I work here for a very long time, I pay tax and for me, if you want to apply for asylum seeker [status], you have to respect the law of this country.

"I didn't come to this country and want to bring my laws from Cameroon to England. No, that's not good and that's why we have a lot of problems. For me, if you want to live here, you have to respect the country and you have to love this country, that's why you stay.

"For me, I love this country and it would be amazing to win a Commonwealth medal for this country. Maybe a Commonwealth gold," she says with a wink. "That's my goal to do my best and win that gold medal."

Ngake would love to add that to her London 2012 bronze – only Cameroon's sixth Olympic medal ever – and one that still remains in the country of her birth.

"The best thing for me would be to go back to Cameroon and take the medal, but I don't want to go back because of the politics there," she says.

But there is another goal on the horizon following the Commonwealth Games - to qualify for the 2028 Los Angeles Olympics.

"Very challenging, but [it would be] very, very special," Ngake says with a smile.

This time, it would be one she could actually hold in her own hands and it would never be hidden away in a drawer.

title: Five things we've learned from first half of F1 season
description: BBC F1 correspondent Andrew Benson analyses the five key things we've learned from the 2026 season so far.
fullText:
Formula 1 teams head off on their summer break this week after a hectic 11 races to start a new era of the sport.

F1 2026 has been full of storylines - controversy over new rules, a new star emerging, the rebirth of an old one, and calendar disruption caused by a war.

Even now, as they head off on holiday for a couple of weeks, the teams still don't know how many races are left this season.

But those so far have revealed plenty. Here are five things we have learned so far in F1 2026.

Kimi Antonelli started his Formula 1 career in 2025 hyped as the next generational talent - but did not live up to that billing in his maiden season.

This was supposed to be his team-mate George Russell's year.

Mercedes have delivered on the expectation they would be the team to beat with eight wins and 10 pole positions in the first 11 grands prix, and Russell dominated his rookie team-mate in 2025.

But Antonelli took a gargantuan step in development over the winter and, while Russell started the season strongly with a win, the Italian soon took control.

Initially, the competitive picture between the two was slightly clouded by some poor luck for Russell in the opening races of the season.

But, as time has passed, it has become increasingly clear that Antonelli is dominating his team-mate so far this season in the best car.

While Russell has floundered a little, less comfortable with the car, and is still afflicted by bad luck, pace seems to flow from Antonelli so easily. Along with devastating pace, his driving is decisive, committed and cool.

The 19-year-old will be tough to stop in the second half of the season.

Russell proud of resilience after string of problems

This year's F1 championship introduced the biggest rule change in the sport's history, with new aerodynamic and engine regulations.

While the chassis rules have generally been a hit - even if the cars are a little slower than last year - the new engines most definitely have not.

The nominal 50-50 split between internal combustion and electrical power (more like 53-47 in reality) combined with the architecture of the engines, has left them energy starved.

And when the battery is empty, the cars have only about 540bhp - less power than a Formula 3 car, but with loads more grip.

The need to constantly charge the battery has neutered many of the best corners on many of F1's greatest tracks, reducing them to what Fernando Alonso has called "charging stations".

The flip side is the energy starvation has led to some interesting battles, known as "yo-yo racing", with cars swapping positions repeatedly over a number of laps.

But the drivers point out this is artificial, and that overtakes are often happening simply because one driver suddenly has 350kW (470bhp) more than the other.

As four-time champion Max Verstappen says: "Sometimes people say: 'Ah yeah, but this was a great race.' I say: 'Yeah, but it's not really realistic the way we are racing.'

"And then you arrive to some tracks and you're driving on not a lot of horsepower for F1 standards. And it's a little bit painful, which I could see coming already for years. So, it's then, of course, not the most exciting.

"At one point I'm also a little bit fed up with repeating myself, because it's already hard enough just having to drive it."

The drivers - especially Verstappen and Fernando Alonso, but most of the others, too - were very vocal about this from very early in the season. The sport as a whole recognised there was a problem, and has reacted.

Tweaks to the rules to lessen the problem were made after just three races, and the engine split will be modified to become 60-40 by 2028, with an intermediate step for next year.

That will significantly reduce these issues, but not eradicate them completely.

F1's governing body the FIA was warned repeatedly in the years leading up to 2026 that this energy starvation issue would happen.

This has left an easy target for FIA president, Mohammed Ben Sulayem, to propose a return to naturally aspirated V8 engines for 2031.

It's an idea with distinctly limited support among F1's stakeholders. It lacks imagination and analysis, comes with its own set of problems, and is effectively turning the clock back 15 years.

The issue is not hybrid engines or turbos per se; it is the lack of energy recovery possibilities.

It's a situation F1 forced on itself by removing the MGU-H, which recovered energy from the turbo and exhaust, and not allowing recovery from the front axle.

The sport needs to take a pause, intelligently and rigorously analyse what it wants from its engines in the future.

Then it needs to come up with a package that satisfies the manufacturers, has road-relevance, embraces concerns about the climate crisis, does not create a noise-hazard threat to some of the sport's most high-profile races, is cheaper, allows the drivers to almost total access to full power, and gives a facility for overtaking.

Lewis Hamilton's career reached its lowest point in 2025, during a maiden season with Ferrari the seven-time champion himself described as a "nightmare".

Hamilton's struggles - in the context of a difficult final season at Mercedes in 2024 - raised all sorts of questions.

He has admitted he doubted himself at times last year.

Hamilton said: "There were definitely moments that I was like: 'Sheesh, maybe it is true that, you know, when you get to a certain point, you lose it.'"

Those comments came in the wake of his victory at the Spanish Grand Prix - the zenith of a first half-season that has definitely proved he has not "lost it".

Hamilton, 41, is rejuvenated this year - back to something close to his best - and the battle with team-mate Charles Leclerc - pretty much entirely one-sided in 2025 - is neck and neck.

He's even sort-of in the championship fight - in second place, 50 points behind Antonelli.

Is this down to the new cars behaving more to his liking than the ground-effect ones of the past four seasons, assiduous work behind the scenes to integrate himself more closely with Ferrari, or the team accommodating some of his preferences into the car design this year?

Even, as his former team boss Toto Wolff has said, "maybe the new girlfriend helps" - a reference to Hamilton's relationship with American media personality and businesswoman Kim Kardashian.

There is still some room for improvement - four penalties in the past three races is very much not Hamilton-esque. But his revival is a relief - for him, and all those who have witnessed his incredible career so far.

On paper, Aston Martin have the ingredients to be title contenders - design legend Adrian Newey in charge, multiple championship-winning engine manufacturer Honda providing the power-units, the legendary Alonso in the cockpit, and ample funding from billionaire owner Lawrence Stroll and Saudi Arabian sponsorship.

But the first half-season of this much-vaunted package has been nothing less than an embarrassment.

Both car and engine were a long way from competitiveness at the start of the season, Stroll was almost in tears when the team's predicament became clear in pre-season testing, and they spent the first 10 races right at the back.

The final race before the summer break, however, provided real hope.

A massive upgrade package based on lessons learned in the early races - increasing downforce and reducing weight - has taken what looks like two seconds off the car's lap times.

Most importantly, the success of the package proved out the team's development tools, which for the past three years had produced upgrades that did not deliver what the team expected.

A new Honda engine is due for the next race - the Dutch Grand Prix on 21-23 August - with expectations it should edge the team forwards a little more.

After the team proved it could improve the car, a lot rests on that engine. "No pressure," as Alonso himself said with a smile after Hungary. It was both a joke and not a joke.

Alonso, 44, is out of contract at the end of the year, and wants to see evidence that Honda, which has finally brought all the expertise behind its championship-winning engines with Red Bull back into the F1 design team, is on the right path.

If it's a step forward, it should significantly increase the chances of Alonso staying for another year - although he still has to convince himself he can enjoy his racing with these engines he dislikes so much.

Alonso optimistic about Aston Martin upgrade - will it decide his future?

For three years after taking over as Williams team principal at the start of 2023, James Vowles had been talking up 2026 as the year the team would make a giant leap towards their ambition of returning to winning ways.

A surprisingly strong 2025 - in which Williams finished fifth in the constructors' championship - seemed to be proof the team were not only on the right track, but even ahead of schedule.

This year, they have had a brutal reality check.

The car was late, overweight by about 25kg, and lacked performance. Williams' first half-season has proved them to be ninth fastest team and nearly 0.4secs on average slower than the team just ahead of them - Haas.

Only troubled Aston Martin and newcomers Cadillac have been slower - and Aston Martin's Hungary upgrade seems to have left Williams as the 10th best team.

And all that with the best engine on the grid - the Mercedes.

Drivers Carlos Sainz and Alex Albon are definitely not impressed - although they continue to say the right things in public.

Vowles has explained the complexities of producing a new car to a new rule set stress-tested the factory and exposed weaknesses that were previously not apparent.

But he said similar things when the 2024 car was late.

Vowles says he's "glad" they have gone through this and insists the team are now making progress.

"Never let a good crisis go to waste," he says. "The amount of changes we have made have put us into a very good situation in the future, and I don't think we would have made them if we'd partially succeeded this winter.

"So, as painful as it's been, I believe we had to go through it as well."
